_provenance.notes: The industrialization of Alaska salmon processing relied on transformative 20th-century inventions. Prior to 1903, all salmon butchering was done manually by Chinese contract laborers at 2-3 fish per minute. E.A. Smith's 1903 invention of the automated salmon butchering machine—controversially named the 'Iron Chink'—gutted and cleaned 60-80 fish per minute, revolutionizing cannery economics and enabling the massive harvest expansion of the 1910s and 1920s.

key_technological_innovations.impact: Established first Alaska canneries at Klawock and Sitka.

key_technological_innovations.invention: Smith's Automated Salmon Butchering Machine ('Iron Chink')
key_technological_innovations.impact: Replaced 15-20 manual butchering stations; increased processing speed by 2,000%.
Eliminated solder contamination; allowed continuous automated filling lines.
Standardized 1-lb tall cans; allowed mass production during 1936 harvest peak.

key_technological_innovations.invention: Flash Freezing & Refrigerated Sea Water (RSW) Vessel Hold Systems
key_technological_innovations.impact: Shifted industry from 90% canned to fresh/frozen salmon fillets and vacuum-sealed portions.
